title: Choirs

segments.voice: Yesterday, organs, guitars and drums, and a psalm that ends on breath. Your line was every instrument praise.

Four people stand in a row, each singing a different note. Alone, the low note sounds gloomy. The high one sounds thin. The two in the middle sound like they've lost the tune. Then they sing at the same moment, and the four odd notes become one chord, full and warm, that none of them could make alone. That's the whole secret of a choir: a cathedral choir in white robes, a gospel choir swaying on the beat, an Orthodox choir singing a service from start to finish, six faithful people in a village church.

Start at the temple. When Solomon's temple is dedicated, Chronicles says: "It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD." Then, the story says, the house was filled with a cloud. The singing comes first; the glory follows. Next, one mouth, many voices. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome: "That ye may with one mind and one mouth glorify God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." One mouth sounds like everyone saying the same thing. But in a choir, sopranos, altos, tenors and basses each sing a different line, and the unity is in the harmony, not in sameness. If everyone sang the melody, you'd lose the chord. Then, a choir on a wall. In Nehemiah, Jerusalem's broken walls have been rebuilt, and Nehemiah sets two great companies of singers giving thanks on top of the wall. They go opposite ways and meet at the house of God: two choirs, singing a city back to life. Last, near the Bible's end, John hears heaven in Revelation: "And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth." Countless voices, each its own, poured into one sound. In this scene, heaven doesn't whisper. It sings.

If someone's with you, hum a tune you both know, a hymn or a lullaby, and listen for the moment your voices meet. If you're alone, hum one part along with a choir recording, the low line or the high one, and notice how it fits inside the whole. If you pray, you can let the song be your prayer alongside other voices; if you don't, listen for the place where many voices become one sound.
Choirs. Many voices, each holding its own part, making one sound to praise God.
Your line: many voices. Each one holds its own part, and the chord needs all of them. See you next time.

howItsDone: Church choirs come in different forms: robed cathedral and parish choirs, gospel choirs, Orthodox choirs that sing the whole liturgy, and small groups of volunteers who rehearse during the week and lead the congregation's singing on Sunday.

fork.setup: you're Nehemiah. Jerusalem's walls are rebuilt, and it's time to give thanks. how do you arrange the singers?
options: one big crowd at the main gate.
two great companies, walking the wall in opposite directions.
a single singer on the highest tower.
fork.reveal: two companies giving thanks set off in opposite directions along the wall and met at the house of God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a choir is the people who sing so the rest don't have to.
what it means: many different voices, each holding its own part, making one sound.
what a scholar hears: Chronicles: the singers "as one, to make one sound," and then the house filled with a cloud. the song comes before the glory.
recall: the talk that opens up the readings
guess: groups singing different parts as one sound
the soloists hired to sing alone at weddings
the clergy who chant the prayers at the altar

chat.says: Why would a choir sing different notes? Wouldn't one tune sound more together?
options: A choir's unity is harmony: each part sings its own line, and together they make one chord.
Different notes are a mistake; the best choirs always sing one melody, all together.
Only the soloist matters in worship; the other voices are just there to fill the room.
chat.meaning: Sopranos, altos, tenors and basses each sing a different line. If everyone sang the melody, you'd lose the chord: unity in harmony.

Chronicles.meaning: Bible books retelling Israel's kings and the temple

Nehemiah.meaning: a Bible book about rebuilding Jerusalem's walls

Alleluia.meaning: a shout of praise to God, from Hebrew

notes: Audit: 'Revelation's heaven is not silent' and the myth 'Revelation pictures heaven as silent' (false) were contradicted by Revelation 8:1 ('there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour'); the teach now speaks of this scene only, and the myth item is about Revelation 19's multitude.
Editor pass: 'Revelation pictures the end' changed, since Revelation 19:6 is a scene of heaven, not the story's end.
Nehemiah 12:31–40 summarized: two thanksgiving companies on the wall, going opposite ways, meeting at the house of God; confirm the summary.
'Revelation pictures the end not in silence, but in song. generalizes from Revelation 19; a Keeper may prefer 'Revelation pictures'.
Hook's list of choir kinds (cathedral, gospel, Orthodox, a village church) is illustrative and unquantified.
Original left null: the Greek choros was avoided under the claims rule (it would invite an etymology of 'choir').
